newsitem.title: USA: Natural gas supplies seen ample for winter.
newsitem.headline: Natural gas supplies seen ample for winter.

text.p: With winter closing in, industry analysts say there are ample supplies of natural gas for home heating, but only time will tell whether there will be a repeat of the skyrocketing prices brought on by last year's record cold and snow.

"The Northeast has plenty of gas, and we're heading into an Indian Summer," said one gas trader, noting that most signs were pointing toward mild weather for the next few days in the East and cooler weather in the West.
Mild weather would allow companies to continue to build up supplies in storage ahead of winter.

Although most winter forecasts are still inconclusive, the National Weather Service in its 90-day outlook is calling for below-normal temperatures for November through January in the Northeast and northern plains west of Chicago.
These colder-than-normal temperatures are expected to continue into February in New England and some of the upper Midwest states, the National Weather Service report stated.
The Weather Service sees 5 percent to 10 percent above-normal temperatures during this period in most of Florida and south Texas.
Some analysts' forecasts, however, call for colder weather in the Northeast in November but then a warmer trend ensuing in December through February.
The next two weeks will be a telling time for the natural gas storage situation.
If mild weather persists, buyers will most likely put substantial volumes of gas into their underground storage caverns, thereby avoiding paying a higher price later in the winter.
If the nation is hit with severe cold, then a repeat of last winter -- when New York gas prices soared briefly to more than $20 per million British thermal units -- is still a possibility.
Gas being sold to New York currently is trading at about $2.80 per million BTU.
The American Gas Association (AGA) reported that as of Oct. 18, U.S. working gas inventories, or gas currently available for sale, stood at 84 percent of capacity, or 2,664 billion cubic feet.
That put stocks 9 percent, or 256 billion cubic feet, below the AGA's year-ago tally.
In the populous Eastern states, storage jumped 43 billion cubic feet to 93 percent of capacity.
